aim8.t: AIM Chapter 8: Medical facts for pilots

reg-cert.title: Certificates and privileges
deeper: Subparts E and F: student, private and commercial pilots
Chapter 1: Introduction to balloon flight training

lesson.idea: **A commercial certificate is what lets you fly for pay.** In a balloon it also lets you teach, and it has its own age, experience and test requirements.
body: Balloon certificates come in three steps: **student** at 14, **private** at 16, and **commercial** at 18, which also needs at least a private certificate. A student may not carry a passenger or fly for hire, and flies solo only with an instructor's endorsement for that make and model, updated every 90 days.

A commercial balloon rating needs at least **35 hours** as a pilot, including 20 hours and 10 flights in balloons and 2 flights as pilot in command. Hot air training must include 10 hours with an instructor (at least 10 flights), two 1-hour flights in the 2 calendar months before the test month, **two solo flights**, and a controlled ascent to **3,000 feet** above the launch site. The private rating needs one solo and an ascent to 2,000 feet.

A commercial pilot may carry persons or property for compensation or hire. In balloons the same certificate lets you train students, endorse them for solo and for their certificate, and give flight reviews, with no flight instructor certificate. Test in a hot air balloon and you are limited to *balloons with an airborne heater*, until gas balloon experience and an instructor's endorsement remove the limit.

Carry your pilot certificate and a photo ID, plus a medical when the flight needs one, and show them to the FAA, the NTSB, the TSA or any law enforcement officer who asks. Report a new mailing address in writing within 30 days. You must log only time used for a certificate, a rating, a flight review or recent experience.

example.setup: Lena is 17, with a private balloon certificate and 26 hours as pilot in hot air balloons over 23 flights. A ride company wants to hire her as soon as it is legal.
steps: The commercial certificate needs age 18, so nothing happens before her birthday.

She needs 35 hours, so 9 more. Her balloon hours and flights are covered; she still needs 2 flights as pilot in command, 10 hours of instruction, the two 1-hour test-prep flights, two solos and the 3,000-foot ascent.
Turn 18, finish the list, pass both tests. To fly paying passengers she also needs a second-class medical.

basics.title: Like a driver's license
basics.body: A learner's permit comes before a driver's license. Pilot certificates work the same way: student, then private, then commercial.
basics.alt: Three keys: practice flights, flights with friends, flights for pay.

basics.title: Each step has an age
basics.body: Balloon student at 14, private pilot at 16, commercial pilot at 18. Each step also needs more logged flying and a test.
basics.alt: Fourteen to learn, sixteen to share, eighteen to be paid.

basics.title: Commercial means paid
basics.body: The commercial certificate lets you carry people or property for pay. In balloons it also lets you teach and give flight reviews.
basics.alt: A private pilot takes friends for free. A commercial pilot can sell the ride and train the next pilot.

basics.title: Carry the papers
basics.body: Bring your pilot certificate and a photo ID, plus a medical when needed. The FAA or a police officer can ask to see them.
basics.alt: Like your driver's license whenever you drive.

lesson.idea: **Being paid is what brings in the medical.** Paid commercial balloon flights need at least a second-class medical, unless the paid work is flight training. Flying privately in a balloon needs none.
body: Since May 22, 2023, using commercial balloon privileges for compensation or hire needs at least a **second-class** medical, even on a paid flight with nobody else aboard. No medical is needed for a balloon student, for private privileges, or for giving flight training in balloons. For paid flights the second-class lasts to the end of the 12th month after the exam month, at any age.

To act as pilot in command at all, you need a **flight review** since the start of the 24th calendar month before this one: at least 1 hour of flight and 1 hour of ground training, including Part 91. One in any aircraft you're rated in counts, and so does passing a practical test for a certificate or rating.

To carry passengers you need **three takeoffs and three landings** in a balloon within the preceding 90 days, as sole manipulator of the controls; from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise, three to a full stop in that same period. Not current? Fly by day with no passengers.

No one may act as a crewmember within 8 hours of drinking alcohol, while under the influence, or at an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or more. Except in an emergency, you may not carry a passenger who appears intoxicated.

example.setup: October 20, 2026. Dana has a paid passenger flight on October 30. Her second-class exam was September 22, 2025, her flight review November 12, 2024, and her last three landings in June 2026.
steps: End of the 12th month after the exam month: September 30, 2026. Expired for paid flights.
Good through the end of the 24th calendar month: November 30, 2026. Fine for now.
90 days before October 30 reaches back only to early August, so June doesn't count.
New second-class exam, and three takeoffs and landings without passengers before the ride. Flight review before December.

basics.title: Some jobs need a health check
basics.body: Truck drivers need a doctor's OK that ordinary drivers don't. Balloon pilots are similar: the medical is tied to flying for pay.
basics.alt: A work permit for paid rides. Friends for free, or teaching, needs none.

basics.title: The medical runs out
basics.body: A second-class medical covers paid balloon flights for 12 months, counted to the end of the month.
basics.alt: Exam in May, good for paid flights through the end of May next year.

basics.title: A checkup every two years
basics.body: Every 24 calendar months you fly and talk with an instructor, at least an hour of each. That's the flight review.
basics.alt: Like a dental checkup: you may feel fine, but someone looks on a schedule.

basics.title: Practice before passengers
basics.body: Passengers need three takeoffs and landings in the last 90 days. Out of practice? Fly without passengers first.
basics.alt: A musician warms up before the audience arrives.

lesson.idea: **The pilot decides whether the balloon is fit to fly; the owner keeps it legal.** That means current inspections, records that prove them, and the right papers aboard.
body: The balloon must carry its **airworthiness certificate**, displayed legibly to passengers or crew, and its registration certificate, now good for 7 years. Fly within the flight manual's limits, markings and placards. Part 31 sets a hot air balloon's instruments: altimeter, rate-of-climb indicator, fuel quantity gauge and envelope temperature indicator. The Part 91 instrument list (powered aircraft) and ELT rule (airplanes) don't apply.

Every balloon needs an **annual inspection** within the preceding 12 calendar months. Carrying anyone but crew for hire, or giving paid instruction in a balloon you provide, also needs an annual or 100-hour within the preceding **100 hours of time in service** (liftoff to the next touchdown). You may run up to 10 hours over only to reach the inspection, and that time counts toward the next 100.

The owner or operator is primarily responsible for airworthiness, including **airworthiness directives**: flying a balloon out of compliance with an applicable AD is a violation. Maintenance and inspection records are kept until the work is repeated or superseded, or for 1 year. Total time, inspection status and AD status (number, revision date, method of compliance, next due time) go with the balloon when it's sold.

A pilot who owns or operates the balloon may do **preventive maintenance**, and with at least a private certificate sign it off: small envelope fabric repairs needing no load tape work, cleaning burner pilot and main nozzles, and swapping baskets and burners listed as interchangeable in the type certificate data. And if an unairworthy condition shows up in flight, the pilot in command must discontinue the flight.

example.setup: You fly paying passengers in your own balloon. Its annual was signed off March 15, 2026, at 412.0 hours. On February 20, 2027, it shows 509.5 hours. Tomorrow's flights take 2.0 hours, next weekend's 3.0.
steps: Passengers for hire, so both: an annual, and an annual or 100-hour every 100 hours.
509.5 − 412.0 = 97.5 used, 2.5 left. Tomorrow fits; next weekend doesn't.
Inspect before next weekend. The 10-hour allowance is for getting to the inspection, not for more rides.

basics.title: Machines need checkups
basics.body: You service a car on a schedule and stop driving if the brakes fail. Balloons too, except the schedule is set by law.
basics.alt: The owner books the checkups; the pilot says no if something is wrong.

basics.title: Papers ride along
basics.body: The airworthiness certificate must be aboard where passengers or crew can read it, and the registration certificate too.
basics.alt: Like the registration in a car's glove box.

basics.title: Yearly, plus every 100 hours if paid
basics.body: Every balloon needs an annual inspection. Flying passengers for hire adds one every 100 hours.
basics.alt: A taxi works harder than a family car, so it gets checked more often.

basics.title: Small fixes you can do
basics.body: An owner-pilot may do simple jobs like small fabric repairs or cleaning burner nozzles, then record and sign the work.
basics.alt: Like changing your own wiper blades: allowed, done the maker's way and written down.

lesson.idea: **You are the final authority on the flight, and the flight rules still bind you.** Part 91 sets your preflight duties, right-of-way, minimum altitudes and lights, with a few exceptions written for balloons.
body: The pilot in command is the final authority on the flight. In an emergency you may deviate from any Part 91 rule as far as needed, then send a written report if the FAA asks. Before a flight away from an airport, become familiar with the weather and forecasts, your fuel requirements, and your alternatives. Part 91's fixed fuel reserves are written for airplanes and rotorcraft, so the propane reserve is your call.

**Right-of-way.** A balloon has it over every other category of aircraft, and an aircraft in distress over all traffic. When two balloons converge at about the same altitude, the one on the other's right has it. Keep looking anyway: the other pilot may never see you.

**Minimum altitudes**, except for takeoff and landing: over a congested area or an open-air crowd, 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet. Elsewhere, 500 feet above the surface, and over open water or sparsely populated areas, no closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure. Never fly in a careless or reckless way.

**Lights.** From sunset to sunrise you need lighted position lights, so a launch before official sunrise needs them. Keep the three nights apart: lights run sunset to sunrise, night VFR minimums use civil twilight, and night currency runs 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. A basket balloon is excepted from the 91.107 seat belt rules, and the 91.147 Letter of Authorization, as written, covers airplane, powered-lift and rotorcraft operators.

example.setup: Your balloon drifts over the edge of a small town. The tallest structure within 2,000 feet of your path is a 140-foot water tower. Beyond the town are open fields with a few farm buildings.
steps: A town is a congested area: the 1,000-foot rule, not the 500-foot one.
140 + 1,000 = at least 1,140 feet above the ground at the tower.
Over sparse fields, keep 500 feet from any person, vehicle, vessel or structure, farm buildings included. The landing exception covers the landing itself, not a low cruise.

basics.title: Rules of the road
basics.body: Drivers share rules about who goes first and how close is too close. Pilots have the same kind of rules, in Part 91.
basics.alt: Part 91 is the driver's handbook of the sky.

basics.title: Balloons go first
basics.body: A balloon can't steer around traffic, so every other kind of aircraft gives way to it. You still keep watching.
basics.alt: A pedestrian in a crosswalk has the right-of-way and still looks both ways.

basics.title: Keep your distance from people
basics.body: Over towns and crowds, 1,000 feet above the tallest thing nearby. Over open country, 500 feet from people, vehicles and buildings.
basics.alt: A 500-foot bubble around every house, car and person. Don't pop it unless you're landing.

basics.title: Lights from sunset to sunrise
basics.body: Before sunrise and after sunset, the balloon must show lighted position lights.
basics.alt: Like headlights at dusk: if the sun isn't up, the lights are on.

lesson.idea: **An accident means death, serious injury or substantial damage, between boarding and everyone getting off.** Accidents, and a short list of serious incidents, mean an immediate call to the NTSB.
body: Part 830 is the National Transportation Safety Board's reporting rule. An **aircraft accident** happens between the time anyone boards with the intention of flight and the time everyone has gotten off, and involves a death, a serious injury, or substantial damage to the aircraft.

A **serious injury** means more than 48 hours in hospital starting within 7 days; a broken bone (except simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose); severe bleeding or nerve, muscle or tendon damage; an internal organ injury; or any second- or third-degree burn, or burns over more than 5% of the body. **Substantial damage** harms structural strength, performance or flight characteristics and would normally need major repair or replacement; small punctured holes in fabric don't count.

Notify the nearest NTSB office **immediately** after an accident, and after these incidents even if no one is hurt: a flight control failure, a required crewmember unable to do the job, an **in-flight fire**, a **collision in flight**, damage to other property estimated over **$25,000**, or an overdue aircraft believed to be in an accident. Include the number aboard, killed and seriously injured.

After an accident, file the written report (NTSB Form 6120.1/2) within **10 days**, or after 7 days if an overdue aircraft is still missing; for an incident, only if the NTSB asks. Until the Board takes custody, move wreckage only to free injured or trapped people, protect it from more damage, or protect the public, and sketch, note and photograph where it lay if you can.

example.setup: A gusty landing tips the basket, which drags 30 feet with everyone aboard. One passenger gets stitches for a cut hand and goes home; another has a simple fracture of a little finger. The envelope has scuffs within the manufacturer's limits.
steps: No. Stitches with no hospital stay aren't on the list, and a simple finger fracture is excluded.
No substantial damage, and no fire, collision in flight, or property damage over $25,000.
No notification required. Had a passenger broken an ankle, that is a serious injury: an accident, so notify the NTSB at once and file the report within 10 days.

basics.title: Something went wrong
basics.body: After a car crash, certain people have to be told. In aviation, the NTSB must hear about accidents and some serious close calls.
basics.alt: Part 830 says who calls the NTSB, when, and what to tell them.

basics.title: Three things make an accident
basics.body: Someone dies, someone is seriously injured, or the aircraft is substantially damaged, between boarding and everyone getting off.
basics.alt: A bruise or a scuffed basket is not an accident. A broken leg is.

basics.title: Some close calls count too
basics.body: A fire in flight, a collision in flight, or over $25,000 of damage to someone else's property must be reported even if no one is hurt.
basics.alt: Close calls serious enough that investigators want to hear right away.

basics.title: Call first, write later, touch little
basics.body: Notify right away, file the written report within 10 days for an accident, and leave the wreckage alone unless people need protecting.
basics.alt: Help the injured, keep people safe, take photos, leave the rest.

sources: 49 CFR 830.2 (Aircraft accident; Serious injury; Substantial damage)

lesson.idea: **Know the airspace class and you know the price of entry.** Each class sets what you need before you go in and how much space to keep from clouds.
body: **Class A**, 18,000 feet MSL to FL600, is IFR only. **Class B**, around the busiest airports from the surface to about 10,000 feet MSL, needs an ATC clearance. **Class C** (a 5 NM core from the surface and a 10 NM shelf from 1,200 feet, up to 4,000 feet above the airport) and **Class D** (usually up to 2,500 feet above a towered airport) need two-way radio contact before entry. **Class E** is the other controlled airspace: from the surface, from 700 or 1,200 feet AGL, or from 14,500 feet MSL. **Class G** is the rest.

**VFR minimums.** Class G at or below 1,200 feet AGL by day: 1 statute mile, clear of clouds. Class C, D and E below 10,000 MSL, and that low Class G at night: 3 miles, 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal. Class B: 3 miles, clear of clouds. Class E at or above 10,000 MSL: 5 miles, 1,000 below and above, 1 mile horizontal. In an airport's surface area you also need a 1,000-foot ceiling and 3 miles to launch or land, unless ATC grants special VFR: clear of clouds, 1 mile, and for a balloon, only between sunrise and sunset.

**Transponders.** A balloon with no engine-driven electrical system may fly in the 30 NM Mode C veil without a transponder or ADS-B Out if it stays outside Class A, B and C and below their ceiling or 10,000 MSL, whichever is lower; it is also excepted at and above 10,000 MSL. Inside Class B or C, or over them up to 10,000 feet, it needs ATC authorization, requested at least 1 hour ahead.

**Special use airspace.** Prohibited areas are off-limits; restricted areas need the controlling agency's permission. An active MOA needs no clearance, but use extreme caution and get traffic advisories from the controlling agency. On a military training route, get its status from Flight Service and keep looking; four-digit routes stay at or below 1,500 feet AGL. TFRs come by NOTAM, and over national parks and wildlife refuges pilots are asked to stay 2,000 feet above the surface.

example.setup: Morning launch from a field in Class G, inside a shaded magenta band: Class E begins at 700 feet AGL. Visibility 4 miles; scattered cumulus based near 3,000 feet AGL.
steps: Class G by day: 1 mile and clear of clouds. Easy.
Class E below 10,000 MSL: 3 miles, and 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal. 4 miles still works.
Stay at or below about 2,500 feet AGL, and 2,000 feet sideways from any cloud you pass.

basics.title: The sky has rooms
basics.body: Picture the sky as a building. Some rooms are open to anyone, some need you to knock first, and some need a key.
basics.alt: A hotel: the lobby is open, guest floors need a key card, the kitchen is staff only.

basics.title: Letters name the rooms
basics.body: Classes A to E are controlled; G is not. Around busy airports you need a clearance (Class B) or radio contact (C and D) first.
basics.alt: B: a clearance. C and D: talking with ATC. E and G: usually just fly in.

basics.title: Keep space from clouds
basics.body: Other aircraft can fly inside clouds. Keeping 500 feet below, 1,000 above and 2,000 sideways gives you both time to see each other.
basics.alt: A cloud can hide an airplane until the last second.

basics.title: Higher means bigger numbers
basics.body: At 10,000 feet MSL and above, the minimums grow to 5 miles, 1,000 feet above and below, and a mile sideways.
basics.alt: Low and slow, smaller numbers. Up high, bigger ones.

sources: AIM 3-4-5 (MOA: contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories)
AIM 3-5-2 (MTR: four-digit routes; status from Flight Service)

lesson.idea: **On a sectional, color and line style carry the meaning.** Blue or magenta, solid or dashed, shaded bands and small numbers tell you where airspace begins and ends and how tall things are.
body: **Airspace.** Class B sectors are labeled in solid blue figures and Class C in solid magenta, as ceiling over floor in hundreds of feet MSL; a Class C ceiling of T means up to the floor of the Class B above. Class D is a blue dashed line, and a minus sign before its ceiling means up to, but not including, that altitude. A magenta dashed line marks a Class E surface area. A shaded magenta band means Class E starts at 700 feet AGL on the shaded side; a shaded blue band marks where a higher floor, usually 1,200 feet AGL, meets Class G.

**Airports.** Towered airports are blue; all others magenta. A star after the tower frequency means part-time, with hours in the Chart Supplement. A thin solid magenta circle labeled MODE C & ADS-B OUT 30 NM outlines the veil around a Class B airport.

**Obstacles and terrain.** An obstacle shows the MSL elevation of its top, with its height above ground in parentheses. The **Maximum Elevation Figure** in each quadrangle (30 minutes of latitude by 30 of longitude) covers the highest terrain or obstacle in it, plus an allowance, rounded up to the next 100 feet: a large 4 and a small 7 mean 4,700 feet MSL.

**Special use airspace.** Prohibited, restricted and warning areas are outlined in blue; MOAs and alert areas in magenta. Most TFRs never appear on the chart, so a sectional never replaces a NOTAM check.

example.setup: You'll cruise at 2,500 feet MSL. Your track crosses a quadrangle with an MEF of large 2, small 9, passes a tower charted 2140 over (390), then runs under a magenta Class C shelf labeled 58 over 30.
steps: The highest thing in the quadrangle, plus an allowance, comes to 2,900 feet MSL. It may stand above your cruise, so find it on the chart.
Top 2,140 MSL, 390 feet tall. At 2,500 you'd clear it by only 360 feet, less than the 500 feet you keep from structures. Climb or pass to one side.
3,000 to 5,800 feet MSL. At 2,500 you're under it; a climb past 3,000 takes you in.

basics.title: A road map for the sky
basics.body: A road map shows highways, towns and city limits. A sectional shows airports, airspace and obstacles the same way.
basics.alt: A hiking map with invisible walls drawn on it.

basics.title: Two colors, two families
basics.body: Towered airports are blue, the rest magenta. For airspace, Class B and D are blue, Class C and E magenta.
basics.alt: Learn it as pairs: B and D blue, C and E magenta.

basics.title: Dashed, solid, shaded
basics.body: Dashed lines mark airspace starting at the ground around an airport: blue for D, magenta for E. Shaded bands show where Class E starts above the ground.
basics.alt: A dashed line is a fence from the ground up. A shaded band is a ceiling over Class G.

basics.title: Numbers tell heights
basics.body: Obstacles show the top above sea level, with height above ground in parentheses. Airspace shows ceiling over floor, in hundreds of feet.
basics.alt: 45 over 20 means 2,000 up to 4,500 feet MSL.

sources: FAA Chart Users' Guide (VFR Terms and Symbols: Controlled Airspace, Class B, C, D, E)
FAA Chart Users' Guide (Airports; Airport Data)
FAA Chart Users' Guide (Other Airspace Areas: Mode C)
FAA Chart Users' Guide (Obstructions; Maximum Elevation Figure; Contour lines)
FAA Chart Users' Guide (Special Use Airspace; TFR)
FAA Chart Users' Guide (Mode C & ADS-B Out 30 NM label; MEF calculation)

lesson.idea: **A balloon goes where the wind goes, so navigation is wind direction, speed and time.** Get the direction in the right north, true or magnetic, and the rest is arithmetic.
body: Charts are drawn to **true north**; a compass points to magnetic north. The angle between them is **variation**, printed on the sectional as isogonic lines: it changes from place to place but is the same on every heading. From true to magnetic, subtract east variation and add west (“east is least, west is best”). **Deviation** is a different error, caused by magnetic fields near the compass, such as steel tanks or radios in the basket.

Winds aloft forecasts give direction from true north; ATIS, ASOS and AWOS voice broadcasts give it from magnetic north. Wind is named for where it comes **from**, so a balloon in a 270° wind drifts toward 090°. Your GPS ground track shows where you're going, so the wind at that altitude comes from the opposite direction.

**Dead reckoning** is distance = ground speed × time, with minutes divided by 60 to get hours. A sectional's scale is 1:500,000, about 6.86 NM per inch, and each minute of latitude is 1 NM. Fuel sets your range: usable flying time, minus your reserve, times ground speed.

A VOR radial is a magnetic line running *out* from the station, so on the 180° radial you are south of it. VOR signals are line-of-sight, so a low balloon may not receive one. Handheld GPS units have no RAIM alerting, so cross-check their position against the ground.

example.setup: Winds aloft at 3,000 feet: 3014. Local variation is 12° E. A good landing field lies 7 NM downwind, and you burn about 18 gallons an hour.
steps: 3014 is from 300° true at 14 knots, so you drift toward 120° true.
East is least: 120 − 12 = 108° magnetic on your hand compass.
30 minutes at 18 gallons an hour is about 9 gallons, before any reserve.

basics.title: A leaf on a river
basics.body: A balloon can't steer. It goes with the air, and you choose a direction by choosing the altitude whose wind goes your way.
basics.alt: Different heights are different lanes of traffic.

basics.title: Two norths
basics.body: Maps point to the true North Pole. A compass points to the magnetic pole, which is somewhere else. The difference, variation, is printed on the chart.
basics.alt: Two clocks in different time zones: both right, but convert before you compare.

basics.title: Distance is speed times time
basics.body: Drive 60 miles an hour for half an hour and you go 30 miles. Drift at 10 knots for half an hour and you go 5 nautical miles.
basics.alt: How fast, for how long? Multiply.

basics.title: Check against the ground
basics.body: Match roads, rivers and towns below to the chart. Use GPS too, but trust it when it agrees with what you see.
basics.alt: Like checking the phone's map against the street sign.

sources: FAA-H-8083-25C Ch. 16 (Variation; Deviation; Basic Calculations; Sectional Charts; VOR)
FAA-H-8083-28B Ch. 3 (Wind Information table: true vs magnetic)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 4 (Atmospheric Circulation: balloons steer by wind layers)
FAA-H-8083-25C Ch. 16 (one minute of latitude = 1 NM)

lesson.idea: **Charts are printed ahead of time; NOTAMs tell you what has changed since.** Check them before every flight, and check the Chart Supplement for each airport near your path.
body: A NOTAM carries time-critical information that is temporary, or that hasn't reached the charts yet. It is cancelled when the condition returns to normal or the information is printed on the chart, and it may be issued up to 7 days before an activity. Get them online through FAA NOTAM Search, or from Flight Service.

**NOTAM (D)s** cover navigation aids, public-use airports, runways and lighting, and airspace activity such as special use airspace, pyrotechnics and drones. **FDC NOTAMs** carry regulatory information, including **temporary flight restrictions**, chart amendments and laser activity. Don't stop at the airport next to your field: the AIM says to check NOTAMs for the whole ARTCC area too, where SUA, TFRs and GPS outages show up.
Most TFRs never appear on the sectional, so a clear chart proves nothing. NOTAM times are UTC (Zulu): from Pacific Standard Time add 8 hours, from Pacific Daylight add 7.

The **Chart Supplement** is the FAA's airport directory, reissued every 56 days. It lists airports, navaids, frequencies and weather sources, plus each part-time tower's hours and what its airspace becomes when the tower is closed (“other times CLASS E” or “CLASS G”).

example.setup: You plan a 7:00 a.m. PDT launch tomorrow 6 miles from Hillcrest, an airport with a part-time tower. Your drift passes a fairground.
steps: FAA NOTAM Search or Flight Service, for Hillcrest and the whole ARTCC area.
7:00 a.m. PDT is 1400Z. A fireworks NOTAM for 0300Z to 0500Z tomorrow is 8 to 10 p.m. local tonight, so it doesn't touch your flight.
The Chart Supplement says the tower opens at 0800 local, “other times CLASS E.” If your field is inside that surface area, you need a 1,000-foot ceiling and 3 miles to launch at 7:00.

basics.title: Detour signs for the sky
basics.body: A road map printed last year won't show this week's road work. NOTAMs are the detour signs.
basics.alt: The chart is the map; NOTAMs are the news.

basics.title: Look them up every time
basics.body: Check FAA NOTAM Search or Flight Service before each flight, for the whole area you might drift through.
basics.alt: Every flight, like the weather.

basics.title: Some are law
basics.body: FDC NOTAMs, including temporary flight restrictions, are regulatory. Fly into an active TFR and you've broken a rule, even if the chart looked clear.
basics.alt: A “no entry” sign that exists only in the NOTAM.

basics.title: The airport directory
basics.body: The Chart Supplement lists each airport's frequencies, tower hours, and the airspace when the tower is closed.
basics.alt: The chart shows where. The Chart Supplement tells how and when.

sources: AIM 5-1-3 (General; Preflight; ARTCC NOTAMs; GPS NOTAMs; NOTAM Classification)

air-radio.title: Radio and collision avoidance
deeper: Chapter 7: Use of a VHF radio

lesson.idea: **Talk briefly, listen often, and keep looking outside.** The radio announces you and gets you into airspace, but most traffic is found by eye.
body: Within about 10 miles of an airport without an operating tower, monitor and talk on the **CTAF**; with no tower, FSS or UNICOM, self-announce on **MULTICOM, 122.9**. The FCC lists 123.3 and 123.5 for uses that include hot air balloons (not advisory service), and many balloonists use them to reach chase crew. Every frequency is shared: idle chatter can block someone's emergency call, and using an aviation radio like a telephone or CB is prohibited.

A self-announcement says who you're calling, who you are, where you are, your altitude and what you'll do, then the airport name again. “Traffic in the area, please advise” is not a recognized call. Below 18,000 feet, say the thousands digits, then the hundreds: 12,500 is “one two thousand five hundred.” Times are UTC: add 7 hours to Pacific Daylight Time.

Class C and D need two-way radio contact before entry. If the controller answers with your call sign, even with “standby,” you have it; “Aircraft calling, standby” means you don't, so stay out. If the radio fails, watch the tower's light gun. In flight: steady green, cleared to land; flashing green, return for landing; steady red, give way and continue circling; flashing red, airport unsafe, do not land.
Scan in short, regular eye movements of no more than 10°, looking at each patch of sky for at least 1 second. An aircraft that holds still in your view but grows larger is on a collision course.

example.setup: Your balloon, N4417B, is 8 miles northwest of nontowered Pine Valley at 1,200 feet MSL, drifting southeast to pass south of the field. Your crew keeps calling you on the CTAF.
steps: Within about 10 miles, the CTAF. At 8 miles you should already be on it.
“Pine Valley traffic, balloon four four one seven Bravo, eight miles northwest, one thousand two hundred, drifting southeast, will pass south of the field, no landing, Pine Valley.”
Move crew talk to 123.3 or 123.5 and keep it short. The airport frequency is for traffic.

basics.title: A shared channel
basics.body: Everyone on a frequency hears everyone else, like walkie-talkies at a crowded campground. One long chat blocks it for all.
basics.alt: Short and clear, then let go of the button.

basics.title: Who, where, what
basics.body: Every call says who you're talking to, who you are, where you are, and what you'll do.
basics.alt: Like calling out at an intersection: “Blue car, Main Street, turning left.”

basics.title: Lights when the radio quits
basics.body: If your radio fails, the tower can signal with a light gun. Green is good, steady red means give way, flashing red means don't land.
basics.alt: Traffic lights, aimed at you from the tower.

basics.title: Eyes beat ears
basics.body: Many aircraft never call on the radio. Move your eyes in small steps and hold each one for a second.
basics.alt: Something that doesn't move in your view but keeps growing is coming straight at you.

sources: FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 7 (Use of a VHF Radio: 123.3/123.5 for chase crew)

lesson.idea: **Stable air resists rising; unstable air helps it rise.** Balloons fly early and late because that's when the low air is most stable, before the sun builds thermals.
body: Air temperature usually falls as you climb; the standard atmosphere uses about 2 °C per 1,000 feet. A rising bubble of dry air cools at 3 °C per 1,000 feet (the dry adiabatic rate); once saturated and making cloud, more slowly, about 1.1 to 2.8 °C (the moist rate).

**Stability** asks what a lifted bubble does next. If it ends up colder than the air around it, it sinks back: stable. If warmer, it keeps rising, like your balloon: unstable. Air is **absolutely stable** when the real lapse rate is less than the moist rate (inversions included), **absolutely unstable** when it's more than the dry rate, and **conditionally unstable** in between.

Stable air brings layer clouds or none, smooth air, and often haze trapped low. Unstable air brings cumulus, showers, turbulence and good visibility. The sun destabilizes low air by heating the ground unevenly, plowed fields, sand and rock fastest, so balloons fly within about two hours after sunrise, or in the hour or two before sunset.

A **thermal** is a rising column of heated air with sinking air around it. Signs: dust devils, a climb you didn't burn for, sudden changes in speed or direction. Caught in one, keep the envelope at or above level-flight temperature, don't vent to force a descent, and wait: thermals are short-lived and usually spit the balloon out higher.

example.setup: At 6 a.m. it's 9 °C at the surface and 12 °C at 1,000 feet AGL. By 10 a.m. the surface is forecast at 21 °C, with 1,000 feet near 17 °C.
steps: Warmer aloft: an inversion. Absolutely stable, good for flying.
21 down to 17 in 1,000 feet is 4°, more than the dry rate of 3°: absolutely unstable.
Thermals are coming. Fly early and be on the ground before the surface heats up.

basics.title: Hot air rises
basics.body: Smoke over a campfire, steam off a cup, your own balloon: warm air is lighter than the cooler air around it, so it goes up.
basics.alt: Heat the air inside your envelope and it lifts.

basics.title: Air moves in bubbles
basics.body: Picture a bubble of air pushed upward. It cools as it rises. What matters is whether it ends up warmer or cooler than its neighbors.
basics.alt: A tiny balloon with no burner.

basics.title: Stable settles, unstable runs
basics.body: If the lifted bubble is cooler than its neighbors, it sinks back: stable. If it's warmer, it keeps climbing: unstable.
basics.alt: A marble in a bowl rolls back. A marble on top of a ball rolls away.

basics.title: The sun stirs the pot
basics.body: Early morning, the ground is cool and the air calm. As the sun heats the ground, warm bubbles start rising: thermals.
basics.alt: A pot on the stove: quiet, then bubbling as the bottom gets hot.

sources: FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 4 (The Standard Atmosphere; Types of Stability; Effects of Stable & Unstable Air; Air Masses; Turbulence: Thermal)
FAA-H-8083-28B 13.2-13.3 (dry and moist adiabatic rates; stability types)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 3 (Weather: fly within two hours after sunrise or before sunset)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 4 (moist adiabatic rate 1.1 to 2.8 °C per 1,000 ft)

lesson.idea: **Fog is a cloud on the ground, made when air cools to its dew point.** When the temperature–dew point spread is small and still closing on a clear, calm night, expect fog by sunrise.
body: Fog is a cloud that begins within 50 feet of the ground. It forms when the air cools to its **dew point**, or when moisture is added until it saturates. Watch the temperature–dew point spread: fog rarely forms when it's more than about 2 °C (4 °F), and is most frequent under about 1 °C.

**Radiation fog** forms over land on clear nights with light wind, as the ground chills the air touching it, and is often densest around sunrise. **Advection fog** forms when moist air moves over a colder surface, often along coasts, and holds in winds up to about 15 knots. **Upslope fog** forms as moist, stable air cools climbing sloping ground, even under cloudy skies. Cold air draining into valleys at night makes valley fog.

An **inversion** is a layer where temperature rises with height. A surface inversion forms on clear nights with light wind, as the ground radiates its heat away. It works like a lid, trapping fog, haze and smoke, and usually mixes out as the sun heats the morning. Climbing out of it, expect a sudden change in wind speed or direction, turbulence, and less lift in the warmer air above.

example.setup: 8 p.m. the evening before a flight from a river-valley field: 16 °C, dew point 9 °C, clear, wind 3 knots. Forecast dawn low: 8 °C.
steps: Clear and calm means strong cooling, while the dew point changes only a few degrees. A low of 8 °C closes the spread to about zero, and cold air pooling in the valley makes it likelier still.
Expect fog around sunrise. Check the spread before dawn, and have a higher launch site in mind or plan to wait for it to burn off.

basics.title: Breath on a cold window
basics.body: Breathe on a cold window and it fogs up. Cool the air enough and it can't hold all its water, so tiny droplets appear.
basics.alt: A glass of ice water on a summer day gets wet outside.

basics.title: Dew point is the fog line
basics.body: The dew point is the temperature at which the air is full of water vapor. Cool the air to it and dew or fog forms.
basics.alt: When temperature and dew point are nearly equal, look out.

basics.title: Clear nights get cold
basics.body: Clouds act like a blanket. On a clear, calm night the ground loses its heat to the sky, and the air touching it cools most.
basics.alt: Frost on the car after a clear night, not after a cloudy one.

basics.title: A lid of warm air
basics.body: Sometimes the air gets warmer as you go up. That warm layer is a lid: fog, smoke and cold air stay trapped under it until the sun mixes things up.
basics.alt: Climb through the lid and the wind can change all at once.

sources: FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 4 (Fog; Fog Formation; Radiation, Advection and Valley Fog; Steam Fog)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 4 (Temperature Variation with Altitude: inversions)
FAA-H-8083-28B 18.1.1 (fog types; spread over 2 °C; radiation, advection, upslope fog)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 2 (Why Do Balloons Fly?: warmer outside air gives less lift)

FAA-H-8083-28B 18.1.1.1.2 (advection fog deepens with wind up to about 15 kt)

wx-fronts.title: Fronts and wind
deeper: Air masses, fronts and local winds

lesson.idea: **Air masses take turns, and the boundary between them brings the change.** For a balloon pilot, fronts, storms and local breezes all come down to one thing: the wind is about to change.
body: A **front** is the boundary between two air masses; pressure usually falls as it approaches and rises after it passes. A **cold front** pushes under warmer air like a snowplow, typically at 25 to 30 mph and sometimes up to 60, bringing towering cumulus, showers or thunderstorms, gusty shifting winds and a quick drop in temperature and dew point, then clearing and rising pressure. A **warm front** moves slower, typically 10 to 25 mph, as warm air slides up over the cold, spreading layer clouds, fog and poor visibility well ahead of it.

In the Northern Hemisphere, wind flows clockwise and outward around a **high**, usually with light wind and fair weather, and counterclockwise and inward around a **low**, with clouds and gusts. Near the ground, friction slows the wind and weakens the Coriolis force, so surface wind crosses the isobars toward low pressure; above about 2,000 feet AGL friction fades, so expect speed and direction to change as you climb.

A thunderstorm cell has three stages: **cumulus** (updrafts), **mature** (begins as rain reaches the ground and downdrafts form beside the updrafts; the most dangerous stage), and **dissipating** (downdrafts take over). The downdraft spreads out as a **gust front**, often marked by blowing dust, up to 15 miles ahead of the rain.
By day land heats faster than water, so a **sea breeze** blows onshore; at night a land breeze blows offshore. Slopes do the same: upslope by day, cold air draining downslope at night.

example.setup: Morning at an inland launch site: wind south-southwest at 6 knots, pressure falling, a high dew point, towering cumulus to the northwest. A cold front is about 45 miles northwest, moving southeast.
steps: At 25 to 30 mph, 45 miles is about 1½ to 2 hours. A fast front at 60 mph: 45 minutes.
Gusty, shifting winds, possible storms, and a gust front that can run 15 miles ahead of the rain.
Don't launch. A balloon can't outrun the front, and landing in gusty, shifting wind is what you most want to avoid.

basics.title: Big bodies of air
basics.body: Weather comes in huge bodies of air, each with its own temperature and moisture: some cold and dry, some warm and humid.
basics.alt: Open the door between an air-conditioned room and a steamy one: the change happens in the doorway.

basics.title: A front is where they meet
basics.body: Cold air pushing in shoves under the warm air like a snowplow. Warm air moving in slides up and over the cold.
basics.alt: Cold fronts: fast and rough. Warm fronts: slow, wide, gray and damp.

basics.title: Highs and lows spin
basics.body: North of the equator, air spins clockwise out of a high and counterclockwise into a low. Highs usually bring calm; lows bring clouds and wind.
basics.alt: High: light winds, clear skies. Low: clouds, gusts, rain.

basics.title: The ground makes breezes
basics.body: By day, land heats faster than water, so cooler air from the lake or sea flows onto shore. At night it reverses. Hills do the same: up by day, down at night.
basics.alt: Hot sand, cool water: that difference drives the breeze.

sources: FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 4 (Types of Fronts: cold, warm, stationary, occluded)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 4 (Pressure Systems; Atmospheric Circulation: Surface Friction)
FAA-H-8083-28B Ch. 19 (gust front up to 15 mi ahead; dust line)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 4 (Convective Currents: sea and land breeze; Anabatic and Katabatic Winds)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 4 (Mature Stage: begins with downdraft and surface rain)

lesson.idea: **A METAR is the weather now; a TAF is the weather expected.** Read them one group at a time.
body: A **METAR** reads left to right: station, day and time in UTC (Z), wind, visibility, weather, sky, temperature/dewpoint, altimeter, remarks. Wind is the direction it blows *from*, in degrees **true**, then knots; G means gusts, VRB a light variable wind. (Spoken ATIS, ASOS and AWOS broadcasts give magnetic direction.) Visibility is in statute miles.

Sky cover is FEW (1/8 to 2/8), SCT (3/8 to 4/8), BKN (5/8 to 7/8) or OVC (8/8), with the base in hundreds of feet **above ground**. The **ceiling** is the lowest broken or overcast layer. CLR comes from an automated station that found no clouds at or below 12,000 feet; SKC means an observer saw none. M before a temperature means minus. A small temperature-dewpoint spread warns of fog.

A **TAF** forecasts one airport, usually for 24 hours. An **FM** group replaces everything before it from its start time. A **TEMPO** group is a temporary change that is more likely than not, lasting an hour or less each time and, all together, less than half of the TEMPO period. An **urgent PIREP** (UUA) reports hazards like severe turbulence, severe icing, hail or low-level wind shear; the rest are routine (UA).

example.setup: Local time is UTC minus 7. Before a sunrise flight you read: METAR KABC 141352Z 15004KT 5SM BR SCT008 BKN025 09/08 A3005. The TAF's next line is FM141600 23012G20KT P6SM SCT050.
steps: The 14th at 1352 UTC, 6:52 a.m. local. Wind from 150° true at 4 knots. Visibility 5 miles in mist (BR is reported only from 5/8 to under 7 miles).
Scattered cloud at 800 feet AGL, broken at 2,500. The broken layer is the ceiling: 2,500 feet.
Temperature 9 °C, dewpoint 8 °C: only 1° apart, so fog could form. Altimeter 30.05.
From 1600Z, 9 a.m. local, wind from 230° at 12 gusting 20 knots.

basics.title: A report is a code
basics.body: Weather reports use short codes so they fit on one line. Each group always sits in the same place.
basics.alt: Like a scoreboard: once you know which box is which, you read it at a glance.

basics.title: Wind comes early
basics.body: Three digits say where the wind blows from, two say its speed in knots. 27010KT is from the west at 10 knots.
basics.alt: A weathervane points to where the wind comes from. Your balloon drifts the opposite way.

basics.title: Clouds and the ceiling
basics.body: FEW, SCT, BKN and OVC say how much sky is covered. The number after is the cloud base in hundreds of feet above the ground. The first BKN or OVC layer is the ceiling.
basics.alt: Cut the sky into eight slices like a pizza. Cloud over five or more slices makes a ceiling.

basics.title: The TAF looks ahead
basics.body: A TAF uses the same codes for the hours ahead. FM means: from this time on, expect this instead.
basics.alt: The METAR is a photo of right now. The TAF is the plan for the day, and each FM starts a new chapter.

sources: FAA-H-8083-28B 24.4.3 (METAR wind, gusts, VRB, sky condition Table 24-4, temperature/dewpoint, altimeter)
FAA-H-8083-28B Ch. 3 wind-reference table (true in METARs; magnetic in ATIS, ASOS and AWOS broadcasts)
FAA-H-8083-28B 27.4 (TAF: 24/30-hour periods, FM and TEMPO groups, P6SM)

wx-forecasts.title: Forecasts and advisories
deeper: Winds aloft, AIRMETs, SIGMETs and charts

lesson.idea: **Winds aloft are your steering chart.** The FB forecast shows where each altitude will carry you, and AIRMETs and SIGMETs mark what to stay out of.
body: The **FB winds and temperatures aloft** forecast gives levels of 3,000, 6,000, 9,000 feet and up. Each code is DDff+TT: direction in tens of degrees **true**, the direction the wind blows *from*; speed in knots; temperature in °C. **9900** means light and variable, under 5 knots. No wind is forecast within 1,500 feet of the station's elevation and no temperature within 2,500 feet, so those boxes stay blank. Speeds of 100 knots or more add 50 to the direction (7315 is 230° at 115 knots); above 24,000 feet the minus sign is dropped.

**AIRMETs** warn of moderate hazards: **Sierra** for IFR and mountain obscuration, **Tango** for moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds over 30 knots and non-convective low-level wind shear, **Zulu** for moderate icing and freezing levels. **SIGMETs** cover severe hazards such as severe turbulence, severe icing and volcanic ash. A **Convective SIGMET** covers thunderstorms, including severe ones: a tornado, surface hail of 3/4 inch or more, or gusts of 50 knots or more.

The **Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA)** replaced the old text area forecast. Ask Flight Service for an **outlook** briefing 6 or more hours ahead, a **standard** one if you have had none, and an **abbreviated** one to update.

example.setup: The FB station near your launch field sits at 800 feet. It reads: FT 3000 6000, then ABC 0807 3114+12. You plan an hour-long flight.
steps: 0807: from 080° true at 7 knots. No temperature, because 3,000 is within 2,500 feet of the station.
Air from 080° carries you toward 260° at 7 knots: about 8 statute miles in the hour.
3114+12: from 310° at 14 knots, plus 12 °C. Up there you'd head toward 130° at twice the speed.
The two layers carry you 130° apart. Pick the one heading toward good fields, plotted from true north.

basics.title: Wind changes with height
basics.body: The wind near the ground often differs from the wind a few thousand feet up, in speed and direction.
basics.alt: Like lanes on a highway moving at different speeds. Change altitude and you change lanes.

basics.title: You go where the air goes
basics.body: A balloon has no steering wheel. You steer by choosing the height whose wind goes where you want.
basics.alt: A leaf on a river goes where the current takes it. Your only choice is which current to ride.

basics.title: Reading the code
basics.body: In four digits, the first two are the direction the wind comes from (add a zero) and the last two are the speed. 2715 is from 270°, the west, at 15 knots.
basics.alt: Wind from the west pushes you east: turn the direction around 180°.

basics.title: Advisories say where not to go
basics.body: AIRMETs flag moderate hazards like turbulence and strong surface wind. SIGMETs and Convective SIGMETs flag severe ones, like thunderstorms.
basics.alt: Road signs: an AIRMET says rough road; a Convective SIGMET says closed.

sources: FAA-H-8083-28B 27.2.1.1 (FB: no winds within 1,500 ft, no temperatures within 2,500 ft of station elevation)
FAA-H-8083-28B 27.2.1.1.1 and Table 27-1 (DDff+TT, true direction, 9900, add-50 rule, sign omitted above 24,000 ft)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 3 (Navigation: directional control through differing wind directions at different altitudes)

lesson.idea: **A balloon rises when the air it pushes aside outweighs the whole balloon.** What sets your lift is the temperature difference between the envelope and the air around it.
body: Heat makes the envelope air expand and thin out. The buoyant force equals the weight of the outside air the envelope displaces; when that is more than the balloon, its load and its hot air, you rise. The bigger the inside-outside difference, the more lift, so cold mornings lift more and burn less fuel.

Every altitude has its own **equilibrium temperature**. Higher air is thinner, so a climb needs a hotter envelope to hold the new level, plus extra heat at first to get the balloon moving. A dark envelope can gain heat from the sun and lose it when a cloud shades it. In a fast descent, air rushing past the fabric speeds its cooling, so a standard burn keeps enough heat in it to stay in control.

Moving air makes lift that heat did not. On the ground, wind over the top creates low pressure and **false lift**; it vanishes as the balloon speeds up to the wind, so launching at bare equilibrium in a breeze can mean sinking right after lift-off. **False heavy** is the reverse: descending into a faster layer pulls the lower envelope down. A shear can also push in the side of the envelope and squeeze hot air out of the mouth (**diminished capacity**).

example.setup: 40 °F at the surface, 52 °F above an inversion at 700 feet AGL. You climb from 300 to 1,200 feet AGL.
steps: 1,200 feet needs a hotter envelope than 300 feet, plus a little extra to start moving.
The air outside warms by 12°, shrinking your temperature difference. Expect to burn more often to stay level.
Under some conditions a dark envelope gains heat from the sun. If a cloud shades it, that heat stops: expect a sink unless you burn more.
The colder air widens the difference again, and the extra lift can stall your descent. Start down early.

basics.title: Hot air is lighter
basics.body: Heating air makes it spread out, so a cubic foot of hot air weighs less than a cubic foot of cool air.
basics.alt: That is why the top of a room is warmer than the floor.

basics.title: Pushing air aside
basics.body: The envelope is huge. The outside air it pushes aside weighs more than the balloon and everything in it, so the balloon is pushed up.
basics.alt: A cork held under water pops up because the water it pushes aside weighs more than the cork.

basics.title: The difference does the work
basics.body: What counts is how much hotter the inside is than the outside. A cold morning gives a big difference cheaply.
basics.alt: On a 30 °F morning a little heat lifts you easily; on a 90 °F afternoon it takes far more.

basics.title: Moving air can fool you
basics.body: Wind over the top of a balloon on the ground adds lift that disappears once you fly with the wind. That surprise is false lift.
basics.alt: Like a kite: it climbs in rushing wind and drops when you run downwind with it.

sources: FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 2 (Physics: Why Do Balloons Fly?; dark envelopes may gain heat from the sun)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 3 (Performance Planning: lifting capacity falls with altitude; Cold Weather Flying: less fuel consumption)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 7 (Straight & Level Flight: an equilibrium temperature for every altitude; Descents: fast descents accelerate cooling)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 6 (Uncommanded (False) Lift; False Heavy; Diminished Capacity)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 4 (Temperature Variation with Altitude: inversions)

lesson.idea: **Warm air at a high field is thin air.** Density altitude is the altitude the air *feels* like to your balloon, and that is what sets your lift.
body: Your envelope lifts by being lighter than the air it pushes aside. When that outside air is thin, the same envelope temperature lifts less. You need more heat for the same load, which burns more fuel and leaves less room under the envelope's temperature limit. Or you carry less.

example.setup: Field elevation 2,600 ft, altimeter 29.70, temperature 32 °C.
steps: Add the conversion factor for 29.70 from the table: 2,600 + 205 = 2,805 ft.
About 120 ft for every degree above standard: 2,805 + 120 × 23 ≈ 5,500 ft.

basics.title: Air has weight
basics.body: A box of air one foot on each side weighs a little over an ounce at sea level. Your balloon floats because it pushes aside air that weighs more than the whole balloon does.
basics.alt: Think of a beach ball held under water. It shoots up because the water it pushes aside is heavier than the ball. A balloon does the same thing in a sea of air.

basics.title: Thin air pushes up less
basics.body: Air gets thinner, or less dense, in two ways: higher up, because there is less air pressing down on it, and on warm days, because warm air spreads out. Thinner air weighs less, so the same envelope lifts less.
basics.alt: Same balloon, same heat. On a cool morning the air outside is packed tight and gives you a strong push. On a hot afternoon it is spread out and the push is weaker.

basics.title: Pilots use a yardstick
basics.body: To compare days, pilots use the standard atmosphere: 15 °C and 29.92 inches of pressure at sea level, getting about 2 °C cooler for every 1,000 feet you climb.
basics.alt: It is an imaginary average day. Every real day is measured against it: warmer than standard, or colder.

basics.title: Density altitude puts it together
basics.body: Density altitude is the height in that standard atmosphere where the air would be as thin as the air you have right now. A hot day at your field can match air thousands of feet higher, and that means less lift.
basics.alt: Ask: if today were a standard day, how high would I have to go to find air this thin? That height is the density altitude.

thy-load.title: Load and gross weight
deeper: Chapter 3: Preflight planning, load and performance

lesson.idea: **Everything aboard counts, fuel included.** Two limits cap your load: the flight manual's maximum gross weight, and what today's air can actually lift. The smaller one wins.
body: **Gross weight** is the whole balloon as it flies: envelope, basket, burner, tanks, fuel, pilot, passengers and gear.
**Empty weight** is the balloon with no fuel and no people. **Useful load** is what is left for fuel and people: maximum gross weight minus empty weight.

Propane weighs about 4.2 pounds per gallon, so full tanks take a real bite out of the useful load. The flight manual's load chart also tells you how much the balloon can lift at a given temperature and elevation. Hot or high days lift less, sometimes well under the certified maximum.

example.setup: Maximum gross weight 1,800 lb. Empty weight 640 lb. Two tanks of 20 gallons each.
steps: 1,160 − 168 = 992 lb, if today's load chart allows that much.

basics.title: Everything has weight
basics.body: The envelope, the basket, the burner, the tanks, the propane inside them, and every person and bag. Add them all up and you have the gross weight.
basics.alt: Picture putting the whole balloon, ready to fly, on one giant scale. That number is the gross weight.

basics.title: The manual sets a ceiling
basics.body: Every balloon's flight manual lists a maximum gross weight. You never fly heavier than that, however good the day is.
basics.alt: Like the weight limit printed in an elevator. It does not matter how strong the cable feels today.

basics.title: Useful load is what's left
basics.body: Take the empty balloon off that ceiling. What remains is the useful load, and it has to cover both fuel and people.
basics.alt: Maximum gross 1,600, empty balloon 600: you have 1,000 pounds to share between propane and passengers.

basics.title: Fuel isn't free
basics.body: Propane weighs about 4.2 pounds per gallon. Three 15-gallon tanks are almost 190 pounds, about one extra passenger.
basics.alt: Every gallon you carry is weight a passenger can't use. Full tanks are part of the load, not a bonus.

sys-fuel.title: Propane and the fuel system
deeper: Chapter 2: Heater system and fuel tanks

lesson.idea: **Tank pressure comes from the propane's temperature, not from how much is left.** Cold fuel means low pressure and a weak flame.
body: In the tank, propane is the same temperature as the air around it; −44 °F is only its boiling point in open air. With liquid and vapor present and no air, pressure depends only on the liquid's temperature: about 25 psi at 0 °F, 93 at 60 °F and 150 at 90 °F. A butane blend gives less pressure and a yellow, sooty flame.

On very cold mornings many manufacturers recommend adding **nitrogen** through a regulator, as the flight manual directs. It raises pressure without warming the fuel, and vapor pilot systems may not tolerate it. If the flight is cancelled and the temperature will rise more than 30°, bleed the extra pressure off through the fixed liquid level gauge. Cold can also shrink seals and O-rings into leaks.

The **fixed maximum liquid level gauge** (spit valve) marks the 80 percent fill. Float gauges are mechanical, can be wrong and often don't read 0 to 100 percent, so plan a reserve. Burn with the blast valve fully open in short burns, not cracked. Check parallel-plumbed tanks **one at a time**, never all open at once.

Propane vapor is heavier than air and pools in low places. Refuel in open air, never from inside the basket or a closed trailer, with no smoking, strikers disabled and the chase vehicle off. When the spit valve spits, close the main tank valve first.

example.setup: Your tanks spent the night in an open trailer at 20 °F. Your flight manual allows nitrogen.
steps: The handbook's table gives propane about 42 psi at 20 °F, against 93 at 60 °F. Full or half-full makes no difference.
Add nitrogen through its regulator as the flight manual says. Pressure rises; the fuel stays cold.
The afternoon will reach 55 °F, a 35° rise. That is over 30°, so bleed the extra pressure through the fixed liquid level gauge.

basics.title: Liquid under pressure
basics.body: In the tank, propane stays liquid because its own vapor presses down on it.
basics.alt: Like soda in a sealed bottle: the fizz stays in while the cap holds.

basics.title: Warm fuel pushes harder
basics.body: The warmer the propane, the higher the pressure. On a freezing morning it may be too low for a strong flame.
basics.alt: Like a can of spray paint: on a cold day it sputters, on a warm day it sprays hard.

basics.title: Quantity doesn't set pressure
basics.body: A nearly empty tank and a nearly full one at the same temperature have the same pressure. The fuel gauge, not pressure, tells you what's left.
basics.alt: The thermometer sets the pressure; the fuel level sets how long you can fly.

basics.title: Vapor runs downhill
basics.body: Leaked propane vapor is heavier than air, so it settles in low spots where a spark can light it. Refuel outdoors.
basics.alt: Picture spilled water running downhill and pooling. Leaked vapor does the same along the ground.

sources: FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 2 (Heater System; Fig. 2-8 fuel system; Fuel Tanks: 80 percent fixed liquid level gauge; Fig. 2-11 Propane Primer; Instruments: float gauges)

lesson.idea: **The load tapes, not the fabric, carry the weight.** Know what each part of the envelope does, read your instruments, and keep the envelope under its temperature limit.
body: The envelope is ripstop nylon or Dacron panels sewn in vertical rows called **gores**. Horizontal and vertical **load tapes** are sewn in and run to a **load ring** at the top center; steel or Kevlar cables carry the basket's load up to the tapes. The **mouth** has a fire-resistant skirt. At the top, the **deflation port** is covered by a panel such as a parachute top; partly opening a parachute is the normal way to cool and descend.

Part 31 requires an **altimeter**, a **rate of climb indicator** (variometer), a **fuel quantity gauge** and an **envelope temperature indicator** (pyrometer), and (31.49(e)) a way to show the pilot the envelope's maximum skin temperature during operation, marked with the fabric's limiting safe temperature. The variometer shows a climb or descent starting or stopping before the altimeter shows much change. Set the altimeter to the briefed setting, or to field elevation if you have none. A wireless temperature link can lose its signal to radio interference or the burner's hot plume.

Maximum envelope temperature is an **operating limitation in the flight manual**. The handbook calls 250 °F the maximum continuous temperature for most balloons, but your manual's number is the one that counts. If a temperature recorder (heat-sensitive dots that turn black for good) or a temperature flag shows the limit was passed, reduce heat and have the envelope inspected as the manufacturer directs before it flies again.

example.setup: At layout you walk the envelope from mouth to top before inflation.
steps: Look for scorching on the skirt and lower fabric.
Follow the load tapes to the cables. Cables must be free of twists, kinks, loose wires or missing sheathing.
Compare any tear with the allowable damage limits in the flight manual.
Check the parachute or deflation panel and its line, and that the temperature sensor is fitted and reads correctly.

basics.title: A bag of hot air
basics.body: The envelope is the big fabric balloon. Its only job is to hold heated air.
basics.alt: Like a paper lantern: the paper doesn't lift anything, the warm air inside does.

basics.title: Tapes carry the load
basics.body: Strong straps called load tapes run up the seams to a ring at the top. The basket hangs from them, so the thin fabric between carries little weight.
basics.alt: Like the ribs of an umbrella: the ribs give the strength, the cloth fills the gaps.

basics.title: Three main instruments
basics.body: The altimeter says how high you are. The variometer says whether you're going up or down, and how fast. The pyrometer says how hot the top of the envelope is.
basics.alt: Where you are, where you're heading, and how hard the balloon is working.

basics.title: Mind the limit
basics.body: Too much heat weakens the fabric. The flight manual gives the hottest the envelope may run; stay below it.
basics.alt: Like an oven dish rated to a temperature: the label is there for a reason.

lesson.idea: **A safe launch is decided on the ground.** Leave room downwind, brief the crew every time, inflate full and steady, and leave only when the balloon is ready to fly.
body: Pick a large open site and place the balloon well upwind of obstacles, allowing at least **100 feet for each knot of wind**. Brief the crew before every flight: expected flight length and direction, positions and duties during inflation, and duties once the balloon reaches equilibrium. Rig the quick-release with little or no slack, the way the manufacturer specifies.

Spread the envelope by handling the **load tapes**, not the fabric. Fan it to at least about **75 percent** full of cold air; fuller is better, keeping fabric away from the flame. Tape strips at the mouth that flutter outward mean the fan needs moving. The mouth crew holds the mouth wide and tall, facing away from the burner. Make eye contact, then make the first burn **short** to check the flame and the crew. The crown line crew leans back and uses body weight.

Upright, run the prelaunch check, including switching from the inflation tank to the first flight tank. If a standing balloon well short of equilibrium starts moving, **deflate**. Only when it is 5 or 10 seconds of heat from lifting off do you have the choice of launching instead. Climbing far too fast can **float the top**: air pressure pushes the top cap down and the balloon descends out of control.

example.setup: An 8-knot surface wind blows toward a power line. Your crew of three has never worked your balloon.
steps: 8 knots × 100 feet: set up at least 800 feet upwind of the line. More is better.
Flight length and direction, each person's inflation job, and what happens after equilibrium.
Fan to at least 75 percent, mouth crew wide and facing away, eye contact, then one short burn.

If a gust shoves the basket while you're far from equilibrium, deflate. Within 5 or 10 seconds of heat from lift-off you may launch instead: add heat for the false lift you'll lose and climb over the line with room to spare.

basics.title: Pick the right spot
basics.body: Launch from a big open field, far upwind of wires, trees and buildings.
basics.alt: Like a runway: the faster you move, the longer the clear stretch you need.

basics.title: Cold air first
basics.body: A fan blows outside air into the envelope until it's mostly full. Only then do you start heating.
basics.alt: Like shaking out a sleeping bag before you climb in: get the shape first, then the warmth.

basics.title: Heat it upright
basics.body: Short burns warm the air inside. The envelope rises off the ground and stands over the basket while the crew steadies it.
basics.alt: Like bread rising in the oven: heat makes it swell until it stands on its own.

basics.title: Go only when ready
basics.body: The balloon should be close to floating on its own before you leave. If it slides across the field before that, let the air out.
basics.alt: Like a car rolling before the engine starts: you brake, you don't hope.

sources: FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 6 (The Crew Briefing; Launch Site: 100 ft per knot; Layout; Inflator Fan Placement, Fig. 6-14; The Crown Line; Safety Restraint/Quick-Release; The Inflation; Prelaunch Check; Launch: floating the top; Uncommanded (False) Lift)

lesson.idea: **Most balloon accidents happen at landing, so plan it early.** Take the first good field, come down at a controlled rate, and brief passengers so their legs act as springs.
body: Landings make up over 90 percent of balloon accidents. Choose a site in this order: **safety** of passengers and of people and property on the ground, then **landowner relations**, then **ease of recovery**. When several fields lie along your track, take the **first** and save the rest for a miscalculation. Get permission before entering private land.

In the classic flare, match descent rate to height: no faster than 500 fpm from 500 feet AGL, 400 from 400, slowing to about 100 fpm and rounding out with a standard burn or two. Below 200 feet, look outside, not at instruments. Cross obstacles climbing, so you can coast over if the burner fails. Watch wires against the background: if they rise in your view or hold still, you're descending toward them; if they sink, you'll clear.

Brief passengers: right place in the basket, face the direction of travel, feet and knees together with knees bent, hold on in two places, stay in the basket. Don't say "brace." Normally everyone stands at the rear; for a high-wind landing, at the front. In high wind, approach the near end of a big field low, brief again, shut off fuel, drain lines, put out pilot lights and vent in time. Tethering a certificated balloon falls under Part 91 and needs a certificated pilot.

example.setup: You're 400 feet up at 12 mph ground speed. Three fields line your track; wires run along the near edge of the first.
steps: You can't turn back, so commit to the first field and keep the others as backups.
As you descend, the wires should sink against the background. If they rise or stand still, add heat now.
12 mph is about 17.6 feet per second, so a 10-second burn response covers about 175 feet.
Passengers face forward, feet and knees together, knees bent, holding on. Slow to about 100 fpm, eyes outside below 200 feet.

basics.title: Plan the landing from the start
basics.body: Early on, look ahead along your path for open fields without wires.
basics.alt: Like a freeway exit: you watch for it miles ahead.

basics.title: Take the first good field
basics.body: A balloon can't turn around. Every field you pass is gone, so the first good one is your best bet.
basics.alt: Like a train: once you pass a station, you can't back up to it.

basics.title: Slow down near the ground
basics.body: Ease your descent as you get lower so you meet the ground gently. Close to the ground, eyes outside.
basics.alt: Like coasting a bicycle to a stop sign: ease off well before the line.

basics.title: Legs like springs
basics.body: Passengers face forward, feet and knees together, knees bent, holding on. Bent knees soak up the bump.
basics.alt: Like landing from a jump: you bend your knees without thinking.

sources: FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 1 (Risk Assessment Analysis: landings over 90 percent of balloon accidents)

lesson.idea: **Fly the balloon first, then fix the problem.** Almost every balloon emergency is a lost vent line, a pilot light out, or a fuel leak, and each has a simple first move.
body: The handbook groups nearly all balloon emergencies into three kinds. **Lost vent or deflation line**: only the burner controls your descent, so stay low and land in the largest area you can, ready for rebound and drag. **Pilot light out**: with two burners, fly on the other. With one, relight with the igniter or a striker; failing that, crack the blast valve (or the backup valve) slightly and light that stream, then land as soon as practical. **Fuel leak**: shut off the fuel source. A small fire at a fitting can then be snuffed with a gloved hand.

Keep control first; check the checklist or flight manual once the situation is in hand. In an in-flight emergency, the pilot in command may deviate from any rule as far as the emergency requires (91.3(b)), and may be asked for a written report.

**Power lines** are generally seen as ballooning's greatest danger. Contact at the basket or cables can electrocute occupants, cut cables or burst fuel lines; contact above the envelope's equator is far less hazardous. If contact can't be avoided, shut off fuel and pilot lights and vent (the FAA pamphlet's word is rip) to come down fast, so the envelope, not the basket, meets the wires. Before flight, fly a torn envelope only if the damage is within the manufacturer's allowable limits.

example.setup: Halfway through a flight in a dual-burner balloon, you hear a hiss and see frost spreading on the left burner's hose fitting.
steps: Check height and vertical speed first. Minor problems grow fast when the pilot stops flying the balloon.
Close the tank valve feeding that hose. Once the little fuel left in the hose is gone, the leak stops.
Fly on the right burner and its tank, and confirm it burns normally.
Pick a good field and land soon. Afterward, review your flight manual's procedure.

basics.title: Stay in control
basics.body: Whatever goes wrong, keep watching your height and keep flying the balloon.
basics.alt: A driver with a flat tire holds the wheel steady first, then pulls over.

basics.title: Most problems have one fix
basics.body: A leak: turn off the fuel feeding it. Pilot light out: relight it. Vent line lost: use only the burner and land in a big field.
basics.alt: At home, if you smell gas, you turn off the valve before anything else.

basics.title: Wires are the big danger
basics.body: Power lines are the worst hazard in ballooning. Stay far from them, and cross them climbing with plenty of room.
basics.alt: Treat every wire as live and every pole as a warning sign.

basics.title: If you must touch, touch high
basics.body: If hitting wires can't be avoided, shut off the fuel and come down fast so the top of the envelope meets them, not the basket.
basics.alt: Better the fabric than the people. An envelope can be repaired.
