lesson.idea: **From sunset to sunrise, a balloon needs lighted position lights.** High flights add oxygen rules: the higher you go, the sooner you must use it.
body: Under 14 CFR 91.209, no one may operate an aircraft between **sunset and sunrise** without lighted position lights, so a launch before official sunrise needs them. If the balloon has an anticollision light system, it must be lit too, unless the pilot judges it safer off.

Supplemental oxygen (91.211) applies to the required crew, which in a balloon is the pilot. Above 12,500 feet MSL up to and including 14,000, use oxygen for any time there beyond **30 minutes**. Above 14,000, use it **the whole time**. Above 15,000, **every occupant** must be provided with oxygen. Hypoxia starts below the legal limits, so the AIM encourages oxygen above 10,000 feet by day and above 5,000 feet at night.

Altitude also costs performance. The envelope lifts less in thinner air, and the burner loses about **4 percent of its output per 1,000 feet**, running at about 88 percent at 3,000 feet, because there is less oxygen for combustion. Plan more fuel and a lighter load for a high flight.

example.setup: You launch 20 minutes before official sunrise with one passenger. You spend 50 minutes between 12,600 and 13,800 feet MSL, then 10 minutes at 14,300.
steps: Position lights lit from launch until official sunrise.
The first 30 minutes need no oxygen; you use it for the remaining 20.
Above 14,000 you use oxygen the entire 10 minutes.
You never pass 15,000, so oxygen need not be provided. With the AIM urging it above 10,000 by day, offering it is still the safer choice.

basics.title: Dark means lights
basics.body: Between sunset and sunrise, a balloon must show lighted position lights so others can see it.
basics.alt: Like riding a bike at night: you need a light even if you can see fine, because others need to see you.

basics.title: Thin air, less oxygen
basics.body: High up, each breath brings in less oxygen. Your thinking suffers first, often before you notice.
basics.alt: Like a candle in a jar: it dims as the oxygen runs low, with no alarm.

basics.title: A three-step ladder
basics.body: Above 12,500 feet: oxygen after 30 minutes. Above 14,000: the pilot uses it all the time. Above 15,000: everyone aboard gets it.
basics.alt: Each rung up the ladder makes the rule stricter.

basics.title: The balloon feels it too
basics.body: As you climb, the burner makes less heat and the envelope lifts less. High flights need more fuel and less weight.
basics.alt: Like a car at a mountain pass: the engine feels weaker because the air is thinner.

sources: AIM 8-1-2 (supplemental oxygen encouraged above 10,000 ft by day and 5,000 ft at night)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 3 (Performance Planning: lift falls with altitude; heater loses 4 percent per 1,000 ft, 88 percent at 3,000 ft)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 2 (Heater System: power loss with altitude)

lesson.idea: **In a water landing, the basket is your float.** Get clear of it in case it turns over, then hold on to it, because a deflated envelope sinks.
body: A water landing changes the passenger briefing. Tell passengers to **get clear of the basket** in case it inverts because of where the fuel tanks sit, then **keep a strong grip on it**, because it becomes a flotation device. Fuel tanks float even when full. A deflated envelope sinks, because it is heavier than water. If the envelope holds some air, the basket may rest on its side for a while; how it finally settles is hard to predict.
On a river, the current may drag the balloon downstream. Generally **stay with the basket**, unless you have landed close to the bank and everyone aboard swims well.

Plan for a long wait over any remote ground. For long mountain flights the handbook suggests water, extra warm clothing or a sleeping bag, a strobe, a radio, a compass, a lightweight shelter and good maps, since the crew may take a long time to find you. Balloon radios are mostly line of sight, so set a "lost balloon" phone contact that pilot and crew can both call.

example.setup: Late in a flight, the surface wind carries you toward a wide reservoir. Fuel is getting low, and the near shore is trees and wires.
steps: Look for a field short of the water, or change altitude to find a wind that turns you.
Tell passengers: once we're down, get clear of the basket in case it tips, then hold on to it. It floats.
Expect the envelope to sink once deflated while the tanks and basket float. Keep everyone with the basket.
Stay with the basket as the current carries it, unless the bank is close and everyone swims well.

basics.title: Avoid water if you can
basics.body: The best water landing is the one you never make. Watch where the wind is taking you and land short of big water.
basics.alt: Like a hiker checking the map for a river before the trail runs into it.

basics.title: The basket floats
basics.body: The basket and the fuel tanks float, so the basket is the thing to hold on to.
basics.alt: Picture a big wooden crate tossed in a lake: it bobs. Hang on to it like a pool float.

basics.title: Clear first, then hold on
basics.body: The basket can flip over in the water. Get out from under it, then grab its side.
basics.alt: Like a canoe that's rolling: get clear first, then hold the edge.

basics.title: The envelope sinks
basics.body: Once the air is out, the fabric is heavier than water and goes down. Let it go and stay with the basket.
basics.alt: A wet bedsheet doesn't float; it sinks and drapes over whatever it touches.

sources: FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 3 (Mountain Flying: line-of-sight radios, lost-balloon contact, suggested provisions)
FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 3 (Navigation: directional control through differing wind directions at different altitudes)

lesson.idea: **Good judgment is a skill you can learn.** Spot the hazardous attitude, name it, and answer it with its antidote before it makes the decision for you.
body: The handbook estimates 90 percent of balloon accidents are human-factors related. Learn the five **hazardous attitudes** and their antidotes: **anti-authority** (resenting rules): *Follow the rules. They are usually right.* **Impulsivity** (acting without thinking): *Not so fast. Think first.* **Invulnerability** (it won't happen to me): *It could happen to me.* **Macho** (taking risks to impress): *Taking chances is foolish.* **Resignation** (what I do won't matter): *I'm not helpless. I can make a difference.* Recognize the thought, label it hazardous, then say the antidote.

**PAVE** finds hazards: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures (like a passenger you don't want to disappoint). The handbook's four risk elements are pilot, aircraft, environment and the **operation**, the flight's purpose. In **3P**, you Perceive the hazards, Process them (CARE: Consequences, Alternatives, Reality, External factors) and Perform (TEAM: Transfer, Eliminate, Accept, Mitigate). Telling yourself it will "probably" be fine means it's time for a reality check. A risk matrix weighs **likelihood** against **severity**.

For changes in flight, use **DECIDE** (Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate) or the **OODA** loop (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act). Beware **get-there-itis** and **peer pressure**. Your crew often sees rain or wind changes first, but the pilot in command is the final authority (91.3). Hand over control in three steps: "You have the flight controls." "I have the flight controls." "You have the flight controls."

example.setup: A group booked for sunrise flies home tomorrow. The TAF shows gusts building by 9 a.m., and another pilot jokes that real pilots launch anyway.
steps: Environment: building gusts. External pressures: the group's deadline and the joke.
Launching to prove yourself would be macho. Antidote: taking chances is foolish.
A gusty landing could injure someone. Mitigate by landing well before 9 a.m., or eliminate the risk by not flying.
The decision is yours as pilot in command. Afterward, evaluate how it worked out.

basics.title: Choices cause most accidents
basics.body: Most balloon accidents come from people's decisions, not broken parts. How you think is safety equipment.
basics.alt: A car with perfect brakes still crashes if the driver decides to speed.

basics.title: Five risky ways of thinking
basics.body: Resenting rules, rushing, feeling untouchable, showing off and giving up. Each pushes you toward a bad choice.
basics.alt: Think of them as five voices. Learn to recognize each one when it speaks.

basics.title: Each has a reply
basics.body: Memorize the answer for each: Follow the rules. They are usually right. Not so fast. Think first. It could happen to me. Taking chances is foolish. I'm not helpless. I can make a difference.
basics.alt: Like a ready reply to a pushy salesperson: you don't have to think, you just say it.

basics.title: Notice, think, act, check
basics.body: Notice what changed, weigh your options, do the best one, then check that it worked.
basics.alt: Like cooking: taste, adjust the seasoning, taste again.

sources: FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 1 (Aeronautical Decision-Making: 90 percent human factors; Hazardous Attitudes & Antidotes, Fig. 1-5; Risk Management, Fig. 1-8; DECIDE Model, Fig. 1-9; OODA Loop; Single-Pilot Resource Management; Positive Transfer of Controls)

lesson.idea: **Your body is part of the aircraft, and it has limits too.** Check yourself before every flight.
body: Before each flight run **I'M SAFE**: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, and an E that FAA books disagree on: the Balloon Flying Handbook says *Eating*, the AIM and PHAK say *Emotion*. The AIM's safest rule is not to fly on any medication unless the FAA approves it; for any new medication, the PHAK says to wait at least 48 hours after the first dose to rule out side effects. Flying while using any drug that affects your faculties contrary to safety is prohibited (91.17(a)(3)). Alcohol: no flying within 8 hours, while under the influence, or at 0.04 or more (91.17); the AIM advises 12 to 24 hours, and a hangover means you're still impaired. The first noticeable sign of dehydration is fatigue.

**Hypoxia** has four kinds: **hypoxic** (thin air at altitude), **hypemic** (blood can't carry oxygen, as with carbon monoxide), **stagnant** (blood not flowing) and **histotoxic** (cells can't use it, as with alcohol). Carbon monoxide comes from internal combustion engines, such as the inflator fan and chase vehicle; it binds to hemoglobin about 200 times more easily than oxygen and takes up to 48 hours to clear. **Hyperventilation** from fright brings light-headedness and tingling; slow the breathing or talk aloud.

Full **dark adaptation** takes at least 30 minutes, and a bright light like the burner flame undoes it in seconds; close one eye when you burn. Look 5° to 10° off center at a dim object. A light stared at in the dark seems to move (**autokinesis**). In fog, trust instruments and fixed ground references, not your body.

example.setup: Festival morning, launch at 6:30 a.m. You had a beer at 9 p.m., took your first dose of a new allergy pill last night, and will inflate in a sheltered corner beside gasoline fans.
steps: 9 1/2 hours meets the 8-hour rule if you're under 0.04 and unimpaired, but it is short of the AIM's 12 to 24 hours.
A first dose last night is inside the PHAK's recommended 48-hour wait, and the AIM's safest rule is no medication without FAA approval. Following that advice, you don't fly today.
Whoever flies should stand upwind of fan exhaust: CO causes hypemic hypoxia.
Today you crew instead of fly.

basics.title: Check yourself like the balloon
basics.body: Before flying, run I'M SAFE: are you ill, on medication, stressed, drinking, tired, or underfed or upset?
basics.alt: You'd never fly with a cracked fuel hose. A tired or sick pilot is a cracked part too.

basics.title: Your brain needs oxygen
basics.body: Too little oxygen, from height, bad air or alcohol, slows your thinking before you feel anything.
basics.alt: Like a phone on low battery: still working, just slower and buggier.

basics.title: Engines make an invisible gas
basics.body: Fans and vehicles give off carbon monoxide, which you can't see or smell. Stay upwind of exhaust.
basics.alt: Like idling a car in a closed garage: the danger gives no warning.

basics.title: Eyes need time in the dark
basics.body: Your eyes take about half an hour to adjust to darkness, and one bright flash resets them.
basics.alt: Walk into a dark theater and you see nothing, then slowly the seats appear. One bright phone screen and you start over.
